utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the next page, the question you just asked me --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We need to bring it up on e-court. We now have 33 on our screens of that chart. Now, move on to the next page, which would be 34 of the English, and in Croatian, what is this?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: This is a chart showing the internal organisation of a defence office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There's another page in English. Yes, now we have it. So this is a diagram showing the internal organisation of a defence office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, does this analysis also mention all the difficulties that the administrations and offices came across?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As we will quickly move on to questions concerning mobilisation, would you please look at page 52 in the Croatian, which is page 40 in English. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment. It starts with mobilisation; right?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where it says what the task of mobilisation was, and then it says that the special passes ensuring that measures of readiness are carried out and constant mobilisation of personnel and materiel resources in order to reinforce and replenish the armed forces and take other effective measures for the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this analysis covering performance in 1993, does it follow that mobilisation work was permanent and constant in the offices administrations for defence?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Some problems encountered in the mobilisation process are mentioned here, out-of-date military records and all the other difficulties mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, those were the main difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It also mentions conscripts who had lived in Croatia before, but their records were kept in our offices. Were there persons in your records who were living in your area but who had volunteered to join units in the Republic of Croatia after the attack by the Serb forces or, rather, the JNA in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, there were such people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, in the course of 1993, did you draw up overviews of the engagement of conscripts in the Citluk defence office, and did you forward this information to the defence administration in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Throughout 1993, we constantly carried out analyses and compiled reports and forwarded them to the defence administration which to the best of my knowledge then forwarded them to the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now look at 1D 1672.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: These are minutes from a meeting of the HVO of the HZ-HB dated the 22nd of July, 1993. Could we please look at conclusion number 1, if you can clarify, which says that the Defence Department shall for the next meeting update the summary of engagement of Croatian conscripts according to the recruitment structures with the number of killed and wounded and update the existing information. Mr. Pinjuh, briefly, these are minutes from a working meeting held on the 22nd of July, 1993. Can you comment on the reasons why a summary of engagement of Croats is required?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, it's quite obvious. We've already mentioned the 30th of June, 1993, and this must be the reason why an analysis is being asked for in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you remember doing such analyses?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that we did do them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look, then, at document P 6017.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, this is an analysis of the capabilities and assignments of military conscripts in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and dated the 22nd of October, 1993, and at the beginning, security and military situation is mentioned. And I will ask you to take a look at page 5 in the Croatian text, which is page 8 in English, because it provides data for Citluk municipality.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes. This is the information I analysed and sent to the defence administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There's an interesting piece of information here in the third line from the bottom in your report where it says HV and RH MUP 19. Can you explain to Their Honours who these military conscripts are?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: These are conscripts who were kept in the records of the HVO, or our office, and who after the aggression on the Republic of Croatia volunteered to join units of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 8, which is page 13 in English. Here we have the total at the level of the Mostar defence administration, and it says that in this administration alone there were --

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: 1.128 military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where, Mr. Pinjuh? Where were these 1.328 [as interpreted] conscripts?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: In the units of the Croatian army and the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, where they were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's all right. The number is in the transcript. Mr. Pinjuh, we will deal with these questions later, but as my time is limited, I would now like to show you briefly several documents referring to meetings held in 1993 in the administrations and offices, and I will ask you whether these documents reflect the problems you came across. Please look at document 2D 1209.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: These are conclusions and proposals from a joint meeting of the chiefs of the defence administrations and offices for defence in northwestern Herzegovina. The meeting was held on the 14th of April, 1993, in Tomislavgrad, and you can see from the issues on the agenda what the problems were, and these were similar in other administrations as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at 2D 995.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I remember this. There was an unannounced inspection by the head -- or, rather, the chief of the administration with his assistants, and there was a report on the situation found in each office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please look at P 6234.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: These are minutes from a session of the Mostar defence administration of the 29th of August [as interpreted], 1993, at which I and one of my officers were present. And you can see that the meeting was also attended by Mr. Bruno Stojic, the chief of the administration for military -- for conscripts, Mr. Barbic [phoen] and Mr. Basinovic [phoen] from the same administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't know whether you said this or whether it's an error in the transcript. When was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: It says the 29th of October, 1993, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pinjuh, we've seen several meetings here, could you tell us, please, whether problems were discussed at these meetings, and what were the problems faced by everyone present in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: This mostly had to do with updating military records, problems of draft evasion, people moving from one unit to another on their own initiative, people joining units on their own initiative, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. At the very outset, you said that the most important tasks dealt with by the administrations and offices for defence were inter alia mobilisation tasks. Can you explain to the Court how mobilisation was carried out in the territory of the HZ-HB, and let's look right away at 2D 1364. And then please explain to the Court what this is about, and I will put more questions to you after that.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: This is a mobilisation proclaimed on the 10th of July, 1992, by the president of HZ-HB, Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, according to the decree on the armed forces, was Mr. Mate Boban the only person authorised to declare mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you explain to Court what you were doing in July 1992, what work you were doing, and whether you were doing anything that had to do with this proclamation of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: As I said, on the 1st of June, I became the administrator of the office, and this mobilisation came as a surprise to me, although we had already managed to put the military records more or less in order. The first thing we did was to call up conscripts aged 18 to 60. We drew up lists of these men and handed them over to the existing units, which had been established as volunteer units in 1991. This job never stopped. Whoever failed to respond was called up again and again in an attempt to get them to do their duty like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I hope it's not a question anticipating yours, but anyway, it's on my time, the Bench's time, so you can only relax about it. Mr. Pinjuh, you have told us previously - now you have alluded to it again - that mobilisation was practically a permanent thing that went on and on practically all the time. Now you have said that Mr. Boban was the only one authorised to order mobilisation. How do we reconcile the two things? I can imagine, but I would like you to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president Mr. Boban pursuant to the decree on the armed forces was the only one who had the right to declare mobilisation. But mobilisation has its time-period and tasks. As we've already mentioned, these tasks, for reasons already stated, could never be carried out fully. They were never completed. That's why they were carried out over a longer period of time than initially envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the document 2D 01364, you see in number 4 that President Boban orders mobilisation must be finished by 18 hours July 11th, 1992. Do we have to understand that this was disregarded practically? This did not work; it was not finished then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that according to what you have said, Your Honour, our reports were sent within this dead-line, but the effect of this order was not good enough so that the order was not carried out fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. That's what I gather from what you told us. And later on, was Boban's order renewed, or was it just continuing in its validity so that you continued to mobilise on the basis of the original order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct. As far as I know, we implemented this order permanently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to explain to the Court why mobilisation was proclaimed on the 10th of July, 1992. What happened when this mobilisation call came?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I remember that it was the time with a fierce attack by the Serb army against HZ-HB, especially the municipalities mentioned in this particular order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, the answer you gave earlier on to me and now to Judge Trechsel, that the business of mobilisation was continuous and that no new mobilisation was proclaimed but you carried on working in 1992 and 1993 pursuant to this came proclamation for mobilisation, I'd like us now to look at several other documents to see what happened next.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D 00847 is the document I'd like us to look at next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, since we are talking about the mobilisation on the basis of these documents, 2D 01374, I'd like to come back to the document we examined before the break, P 00680, which referred to the Home Guards. And here in that document, it states under Article 7 that the head of the Department of Defence also had the right to mobilise Home Guards in particular. Is this the same mobilisation, and does it mean that the head of the Department of the Defence had an equivalent privilege, so to speak, as President Mate Boban regarding mobilisation, except that in the case of Mate Boban, it was the mobilisation of the armed forces, whereas for the head of the department for defence, it was the mobilisation of Home Guards? I'm not quite sure how that's been translated into French.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but may I be of assistance and indicated to the witness that what Judge Mindua is asking you referring to Article 7 of the establishment of the Home Guards, Mr. Pinjuh, you have it on e-court. On the screen in front of you, you have Article 7, so that's what the Judge is asking you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So what is stipulated in Article 7? Was that the task of mobilisation, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No, it's not the same thing. Well, in this document we are dealing with the establishment of the Home Guard units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Home Guard was part of the armed forces, the HVO; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. However, older people were in the Home Guards, as we said, and we spoke about their task, so that's why this relates to the establishment of separate Home Guard units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, what you've just been asked by the Judge, he is linking up mobilisation or, rather, bringing mobilisation into connection with the term used in Article 7 where it says that the head of the Defence Department shall have the authority to prescribe regulations and draw up mobilisation plans for the Home Guard. Does this have anything to do with the very act of mobilisation? I think that's what the Judge was linking up.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've just explained that to us, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, I'm going back to document 2D 00847, and we are continuing our discussion about mobilisation. So in order do that, let's look at the conclusions made in this document. I think that it's on page 2 in both versions where it says: "The Defence Department of the HZ-HB and the Main Staff of the HVO shall undertake all military mobilisation measures in order to provide full protection for Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, my question to you is this. That was point 1 of the conclusions. The first point of the conclusions on e-court, please. Yes, we have 1. We are just interested in point 1. Now, Mr. Pinjuh, can you explain to the Court what these measures are, and were they the measures that you referred to when speaking about the continuation of mobilisation, and did you receive these conclusions? The document is 2D 00847. That's the document number, for the record. Yes, go ahead, please. Answer that.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: This deals with steps and measures that we took continuously, so it's not a question of any new mobilisation. It's continuous.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, did you receive through the defence administration conclusions of this kind in order to continue with your work in the area of mobilisation and do what you needed to do and what hadn't been done yet?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And these were conclusions for the defence office to take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, take a look at document P 2575, which are the minutes from an HVO HZ-HB session and the HVO for Mostar municipality dated the 31st of May. The previous one was dated the 19th of April, 1993, whereas this is the 31st of May, 1993. And I'm going to show you the documents in chronological order so that we can see whether these affairs with mobilisation were done under 1993, and under the conclusions here, if we look at the conclusions - it's on page 1 of the English and Croatian - it says that the Defence Department of the HVO HZ-HB shall be continued as well as recruitment. So was this what you did continuously throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's look at the next document, which is P 2707.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you like to comment and tell us what this decision is? It's the 10th of June, 1993. That's the date. It's a decision. What about?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Once again, it says decision on carrying out mobilisation, which means continuous, and in Article 1 it refers to all non-mobilised men of military age, et cetera, et cetera. So that is a continuation of the affairs we discussed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you now take a look at the next document, which is 2D 1485.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And this is an order from Mr. Stojic dated the 18th of June, based on the decision by the HZ-HB government and which refers to additional mobilisation for military conscripts in the municipalities of Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Grude, Ljubuski, and Posusje.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Yes, Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Grude, Ljubuski, and Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And since mention is made of Citluk, could you explain to us why it was necessary on the 18th of June to issue an order like this, and we saw the ones earlier on.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, quite obviously in these particular municipalities, mobilisation had not been implemented properly, so they are being asked to effect mobilisation additionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the next document, which is P 3024, and we saw this document in the courtroom. We've seen it before. This is 12 days after the previous order, and this one relates to just the HVO of Posusje. Can you tell me why this decision was passed?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, because of the well known events of the 30th of June that we mentioned earlier on, and Posusje municipality quite obviously did not implement the previous orders as it should have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I've just been told that I have 12 more minutes at my disposal, and I have two areas to get through which I think are fairly important, so I'd like to ask you if possible to move through the documents a little quicker. Look at 2D 1233 first, please. They are documents which had to do with mobilisation, and can we just have your comments.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: This is another way in which those who had not responded to the mobilisation call could do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here we have a document that you signed, 2D 1224.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: It's the same thing here except the names of the people are mentioned, names of people to responds to the call-up and the names of those who were placed at the disposal of the Defence Department who had returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you comment, 2D 1234, the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Once again, a public invitation sent through the media stating that anybody who had failed to respond to the mobilisation call should do so and report for duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we have your comments on P 3038 now, please. This is a public announcement signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic dated the 30th of June, 1993, and it comes after the event that we mentioned here a number of times. We have here Mr. Stojic's order, which says that all military recruits in Herceg-Bosna regardless of where they are must report to the defence offices, the nearest defence offices or report to their units and municipalities. Is this a proclamation of mobilisation, or is it a continuous implementation of the mobilisation process as you have already explained to us?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: It's just a continuation of the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. So we can round up this topic of mobilisation. Tell us, please, was it carried out in a satisfactory way until the end of 1993, and I mean mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it was, no. It could have been done in a much better way, accomplished in a better way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, in the mobilisation procedure and bringing the manpower level up to a full complement, were there activities of unauthorized bodies trying to mobilise people in HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I did hear about certain examples whereby the units themselves mobilised people directly, and it wasn't an isolated case either.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you hear that the HVOs in the municipalities, in individual municipalities did mobilisation work, although they didn't have the power to engage in those affairs? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, there were such examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we take a look at document P 01831.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just tell me whether that is a document which confirms what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, because the Mostar municipality cannot proclaim a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, skip over the next document, and look at P 15500 next, please, and tell me whether the municipal government of the HVO of Mostar could on the 25th of February, 1993, pass a decision on the establishment of Home Guard units.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No, this goes beyond its powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And one more document, which is 1D 110 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. You just said that this was not under his powers. Why is it that Mr. Topic, whose name is seen in many document, why is it that he intervenes here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not quite sure. He refers to the Statute. He refers to the Statute of Mostar municipality and relies on that, although there's no logic for him to make decisions linked to the mobilisation process, either mobilisation of materiel and technical equipment or manpower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. If Mr. Topic interferes in the -- in the responsibilities of the Department of Defence, does that have a political meaning or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure how far this was important. I really can't say. I apologise, but I really can't say either way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Madam Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, the proclamation of mobilisation for a materiel tech -- or equipment of manpower, did that come under the remit of the Defence Department or the president of the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Only under the authority of the president of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have five more minutes, so let's try to get through the last area as quickly as possible, and I'd like you to go back to the recruits who were on the list for military recruits in your municipality, and we looked at P 6017, and they were in units of the Croatian army and MUP of the Republic of Croatia. I'm now going to show you a document -- well, skip over one document and find P 3336 and tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a letter signed by Mr. Stojic, and it is addressed to the defence minister, Mr. Susak, defence minister of Croatia and the Minister of the Interior, and it has to do with military recruits who unlawfully are in the Republic of Croatia, and he says they should be sent to the collection centre in Grude. Mr. Pinjuh, according to your records, in your offices, defence offices, did you draw up lists of persons -- the document is P 336. 5336. P 5336. Did you draw up the lists of these recruits who were spending time unauthorised elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe that when it came to the numbers and figures, this is the result of the report sent through the offices to the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to look at P 2647, please.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a letter sent by Mr. Stojic of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia to the personnel department asking that the status in the 4th Brigade be resolved and enabling them to stay with us, and three persons are mentioned: Zlatko Jarkic, Stojan Musa, and Ivan Sabljic. Mr. Pinjuh, do you know these persons personally, and did you have -- or your office for defence in Citluk, did you participate at all in the compilation of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I know all three persons. All three had been pupils or students of mine. I know that after they were wounded in the Republic of Croatia, they spent a time recuperating on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna from where they had gone to join the Croatian army, and they were still kept on the records of the Citluk defence office where they reported while they were there. In the meantime, their unit in the Republic of Croatia asked for them back, and they said they would declare them to be deserters if they didn't come back. They were willing to help, but their status had to be resolved, which is why I sent a letter to the chief of the administration, who evidently forwarded it to the head, and he sent it to the personnel administration of the Republic of Croatia, and I know that this was resolved in a positive way and that they remained for awhile in the units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's go back a little bit because some things need to be clarified. These three persons, if I understood you correctly, were on the records of the Citluk defence office because they came from that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did these three persons volunteer to join the units of the Croatian army when the aggression of the JNA against Croatia began?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did these three persons later answer the call-up they received from your office as members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did they ask through you, and you through the administration, and the head of the department Stojic that their status in the 4th Brigade of the Croatian army be resolved from where they had left in order to join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. And finally, let's look at the next two documents. 2D 1239. Just tell Their Honours what this is about.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, this is a certificate issued by the defence office to every conscript at his request confirming that Stojan Musa in this case was a member of the office or, rather, was -- that his name was in the military records of the Citluk defence office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And Stojan Musa is the same person mentioned in the previous document P 2647; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you please look at the next document, which is 2D 1240.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: It's about the same thing, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just wait a little, please. Yes, go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: It's also a certificate in this case for Ivan Sabljic stating that his name is in the records of the Citluk defence office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We don't have any information about Zlatko Jarkic, but can you confirm that his name was also on the records of your defence office and that he was a conscript obliged to respond to a call-up from the Citluk office?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, to the best of your knowledge, were there also Muslims who went to join the Croatian army as volunteers in the beginning of 1991, that is after the JNA aggression against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know whether some of these Muslims came back to join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina [Realtime transcript read in error, "Army of Republika Srpska"] and whether they had to go through the same procedure of regulating their status, their previous status in the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They had to go through the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And my last question for the witness: Did you have in 1992 and 1993 any direct contacts with Mr. Bruno Stojic? How often and on what occasions?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: In this period, we could have had only a few official meetings, which the gentleman attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, did anyone in the course of your work in 1992 and 1993 ask you to do anything contrary to the regulations or to your conscience?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pinjuh. Thank you, Your Honours, I have concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica. Now, a very short follow-up question, if I may, for you, Witness. Those three people, you knew them well because they were your students, so you have a good memory, Mr. Musa, Mr. Sabljic, and Mr. Jarkic. There are three of them. So if I understood you properly, these three persons entered the Croatian army as volunteers, but when they became members of that army, what nationality were they? What nationality were they at that time? Were they citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or were they Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so they went to Croatia as volunteers, I assume to fight the Serbs because they were injured. They must have been injured during combat with the Serbs; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until now, this all seems very logical, but something surprised me earlier on. You said that they risked being deserters in Croatia. They were not Croatian, so how could they become deserters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their unit would have considered them volunteers because they had left that unit. After their recovery, they were supposed to rejoin the unit and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Would have considered them deserters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they wanted their status to be put on hold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A last technical question, if I may. As far as you know, these three students, your own students, when they entered the Croatia army, did they have a contract with the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as far as you know, yes. Well, before we have the break, there are still 25 minutes, the cross-examination for the other counsel, as well, D3 to begin with or, rather, D1, whatever you prefer. I don't really know who does what anymore. D1.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Dr. Prlic has no questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. D3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of General Praljak will be the first to take the floor, as the Defence of Mr. Prlic has said they have no questions. We have just a brief question, which is of a mostly military nature, and if I may be allowed to ask leave for General Praljak to put the question himself. Cross-examination by the accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a brief question, to the best of your knowledge, did the Yugoslav People's Army attack Croatia without attacking Bosnia-Herzegovina, or did they have a plan to attack all the peoples who were hindering the implementation of its idea to take all the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and aligning Croatia, Karlobag, Virovitica, and so on, Karlovac, Karlobag, and Virovitica, up to the sea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can confirm with certainty that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: According to what you know, it was the peoples, the Muslims, the Croats, whether they were called Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croats in Croatia, as well as Hungarians, and Ukrainians, and Slovaks, who were on the territories which the Serbian political and military ideas considered to be Serbian lands?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, all territories were attacked where there were Serbs. Rather, all those who were not Serbs living on territories where there were Serbs were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the Serbian political and military leadership considered that any area where even a small number of Serbs lived or even no Serbs were actually Serbian lands?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My second question: Are you aware that in the April 1992 I arrived in the areas of Citluk, Capljina, and so on, Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I know that you arrived, but as to the month ...

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you tell Their Honours whether mobilisation and bringing the units up to manpower level was the most difficult job that you, Bruno Stojic, Mate Boban, Slobodan Praljak, or anyone else had to perform in that area to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell Their Honours the following: If you called up some people who had given false addresses, left on their own initiative, gone to Germany or Croatia or somewhere else, or got hold of certificates saying they were unfit and so on, so if only 50 percent, 60 percent, or 30 percent of the men you had called up responded, what legal or other means did you have to take any sort of action against those who had not responded, although they were bound to do so by law, so what could you, Mate Boban, or Bruno Stojic do to those people?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Almost nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll repeat the end of my question. So throughout the war, throughout the war, if you sent call-up papers, sent them out, and 50 percent, 60 percent, 30 percent of the men responded, what could you do to those who had failed to respond? What punishment, what sanctions could you impose, or what could be done pursuant to the laws and regulations in force?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: There was nothing we could do, to put it in a nutshell. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. One moment. I have a question. Following the questions raised by General Praljak, I was listening to both the questions and answers and looking at document P 6017, which is in binder number 2. Now, what I was interested in was page 2 concerning the situation of the municipality of Tomislavgrad. Now, in that municipality - there's no point in looking at the document; you can rely on what I'm saying - there are 27.347 citizens, Croatians; 7.716 conscripts, military conscripts. Now, what I see is that abroad there are some 3.105 people, 3.105, in other words, almost half of the number of the conscripts. So General Praljak when he raised his question was highlighting that. But how is it that Tomislavgrad, that municipality could get these 3.105 people to return? These people were abroad in Denmark, Hungary, perhaps in Switzerland or France. They were working. They had gotten married, had children at school, and so on. How could those people return, take up arms, whereas they -- they were making Volkswagon automobiles in a factory in Germany or something like that? Things are not as simple as they might look. What were the means that you had at your disposal, you yourself, to get these people to return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At municipal level, including the municipality of Tomislavgrad, the municipality could issue a local decision on their material obligation. These were people who had work permits who had left for foreign parts before the war. Many had taken their families with them, and they would probably stay there throughout their working lives. Therefore, there could be no repression applied, nor was any applied to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, my question applied to Tomislavgrad, but if you look at Livno, the same applies at Livno. There were 28.456 Croatian citizens, 9.312 military conscripts, and we see that 3.409 are Livno Croatians that are living abroad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are two examples of municipalities where most of the male population was working abroad, most males were working abroad, and two municipalities where only during the summer would you be able to see the proper number of children and men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the afternoon, I also saw a document that mentioned these conscripts, and in that document it was stated that a non-negligible percentage hadn't actually done their military service in the JNA or else had only entered military service for ten months. The HVO, was it confronted with this problem of qualification of the conscripts in as much as many of them hadn't done their military service at all and those that had hadn't done it for very long? Was that a true problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly it was a problem because nobody was prepared enough for war, especially not young people. But it was difficult, young men who were already in the units, it was difficult to send them back for training, basic and specialised training courses, so they preferred staying on in the units, and then a Solomon's solution [as interpreted] was found to be reservists and then from a reservist's position to go back to being active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question. This analysis of the conscripts, well, in this document I was struck when I looked at the detail of the statistics. I was struck by the number of criminal proceedings that had been taken on a municipality-by-municipality basis. For instance, in Tomislavgrad, 410 criminal reports; Livno, 501; Posusje, 307; Hana Prozor [phoen], 307; Kupres, 167 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or 166, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Uskopic [phoen], 256-66; Bugojna, there were none there; Jablanica, nothing is indicated; Mostar, 147; Siroki Brijeg, 46; Ljubuski, 147; Capljina, 58; municipality of Mostar, now, this is a record figure, 1.056, 1.056; Neum, 26; Stolac, 74; Rude [phoen], 107. Well, these figures seem to be fairly significant. According to you, all these proceedings taken against conscripts, what was the cause of these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the cause was the resistance to respond to the call-up and to do military service, so this is an attempt, well, at intimidation because as far as I know all this remained dead letter on paper. So we did say what we wanted, but there was no way in which we could force them to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These figures, and it seems to be -- 1.671, were they also -- did this include criminal proceedings that had nothing whatsoever to do with the failure to carry out one's military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic for D3.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, good afternoon to you too. I have two groups of very short questions on behalf of the Petkovic Defence. The first group of questions will relate to the questions raised by Judge Antonetti about the engagement of the Home Guards in securing prisons, providing security for prison, and this was recorded on page 31 of the transcript. And then, Mr. Pinjuh, I shall be asking you a few questions about the answer you gave about the two offices within the Main Staff. The first -- or, rather, department. The first was for manpower levels and the second for additional training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, perhaps it would be preferable to take our break now, which will give you an opportunity to start up again after everybody has had a rest. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just I have to intervene. On page 64 of the transcript, line 6, in my question, it said the Army of Republika Srpska. Well, it's being corrected. My colleague tells me it should be the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's being corrected, but as I'm on my feet, I thought I'd just say what I wanted to, so if it's being corrected, then that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Pinjuh, as I said, my question -- first question will relate to the Home Guards, and as Judge Antonetti asked a question about this, the involvement of the Home Guards with respect to securing certain prisons. I'd like to look at a document now in my binder. P 1424 is the document number. 1424 is the number. That's right. It's a document which you've already looked at today, and you discussed it with my learned friend Ms. Nozica. It is an order from Mr. Bruno Stojic dated the 5th of February [Realtime transcript read in order, "15th of November"], 1993, which relates to unit mobilisation changes and in respect of the Home Guards, and I'd like us to take a look at the statement of reasons or explanation of the order, as it says. I'd like to put the date right also. It says the 15th of November in the transcript. I said the 5th of February, 1993, and in the statement of reasons it says that the Home Guard units are being established in order to protect the territories and facilities of special significance for the defence and to provide support to the armed forces. Is that roughly what you yourself said, that the Home Guards were in fact units, relatively older people, designed to protect territories and safe-guard certain facilities and features; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's look at point 2, which defines the special interest features of special interest and significance to defence. I don't need to read through them because we can all do that ourselves. But tell me, please, Mr. Pinjuh, among those facilities, if I'm reading this correctly, there's no mention of any prisons; right?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No, there is no mention of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, it says there that the features of special importance, special significance can be, during a state of war, facilities which are deemed such by the head of the Defence Department or the chief of the Main Staff or commander of the operative zone. Now, Mr. Pinjuh, do you know any decisions or orders or any other documents whereby one of the authorised persons mentioned would define a prison as a facility of special significance to be guarded by the Home Guards?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, let's take a look at page 1 of the document again and focus on 1.2 where it says that the command of the Home Guards, the Home Guard command, along with the municipality HVOs and operative zones evaluate the situation on the territory and determine facilities of special significance for the defence. And in this connection, my question to you, Mr. Pinjuh, is this: Theoretically, did the possibility exist for some municipal HVO in agreement with the municipal units, whether the Home Guards or a municipal brigade, could they decide to proclaim a feature, a facility for special defence and then decide to engage the Home Guards for providing security for that facility? Could that happen theoretically?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I can't really comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, a brief explanation, Mr. Pinjuh, with respect to the answers you gave with respect to the Main Staff. And the two departments, the first department that you mentioned was the manpower level reinforcement, and this was recorded on page 36 of the transcript, and then mention was made of the department for education and training on page 42 of the transcript. And about the formation of the Main Staff, you discussed that on the basis of document -- well, it's not in my number, but anyway, the number is P 00502, the formation of the Main Staff or establishment of the Main Staff, and it is a document compiled in September 1992. Now, taking that document and your statements about the existence of two departments within the Main Staff, one might gain the impression that the Main Staff was a very impressive body at that time. So I'm going to show you a number of documents now about the Main Staff members, and perhaps we could comment the work of the Main Staff which undoubtedly took part in implementing these two tasks that were mentioned, significant ones, in the examination-in-chief. Look at 2D 1352 now, please. 2D 1352. And that's the last document in this set of documents, in my binder. It is a list of persons in the Defence Department in the Main Staff for salaries. It's a salary list for 1992. And the last document relates to the Main Staff. So take a look at that, please. So it's a list of salaries for November 1992 for Main Staff members. The document was compiled on 17th of December, 1992, signed by the chief of the Main Staff Milivoj Petkovic, and here we see that in the Main Staff, on the salaries there, we have 20 persons. Have you found the document? It's the last document. Just look at the Croatian documents. The number at the bottom is 2D 66-0134. It's the last page both in Croatian and English. Have you found that? Have you managed to find it? Mr. Pinjuh, see it says Main Staff, 20 persons. Is that what it says in the document?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, part of the document is illegible, but perhaps we'll manage to decipher something. Tell me, did you know how many people worked in the Main Staff in December 1992 roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, are any of the names familiar on the list? For example, number 8, Zvonimir Susec, have you ever heard of him? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us who he was.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: He was -- he worked in the Main Staff, and I think that he worked in the area of manpower level reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is Zvonimir Susec. Now let's look at another document, Mr. Pinjuh, and I'll repeat the name again. Zvonimir Susec, S-u-s-e-c. Zvonimir Susec. Well, we'll have the next document, and the name is clearly written there. It's P 1579, which is a telephone directory dated March 1993, and under number 4, we have a list for the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Could you tell me the number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P 1572 is the number. Number 1, the Defence Department, and then point 4, the Main Staff of the HVO of Mostar. Look at that list. You will find them on the following page, as well, and somewhere in the middle it says Zvonimir Susec. Mr. Pinjuh, from this list can we conclude that in that establishment department, there's just this one person, the chief Zvonimir Susec?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. In the minutes, yes, but I can't confirm that that was actually the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you that on the basis of this list.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, you said this was a telephone directory, whereas a military formation is something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Formation establishment. Does that mean the actual manpower level, or does establishment mean a systemisation of the work post regardless of how many people were going to employ in a given institution?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I think that establishment when it comes to the Main Staff and the operative zones, military territorial staffs didn't lack carters, didn't lack manpower according to my experience, but I can't say anything based on telephone numbers and telephone directories.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We've just seen the telephone directory, but we also saw the payroll for November 1992, and on that list were 20 persons. Here now, you are looking at this document. Let's see one more document, and then I'll ask you the question. The document is P 1683.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have examined this telephone directory carefully. According to what you remember in Citluk, how many telephones did you have? You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I said that you had two, the 08850082 and 5080582 and 584, that you had two telephone lines, what would you say? Is it true? And did the telephone function correctly, or did it not work very well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was down -- the line was down from time to time, but for the most part it functioned properly with interruptions; the lines were interrupted; there was a lot of digging going on and so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, let's look at the next document. P 1683 is the number. It is a list of members of the Main Staff compiled on the 18th of March, 1993, signed by Brigadier Petkovic. Have you found the document? Mr. Pinjuh, of course you can't compare that to a telephone directory in order to see whether it's correct, but can we conclude that in the Main Staff at that point in time together with the driver, the secretary, the adjutant, the typist and so on, there were 32 persons? There was one whose position had not been regulated yet and temporarily employed in the Main Staff, two more persons. Is that what follows on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we can see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I think we have to say that for the two individuals who were employed temporarily, were two Croatian officers, Miro Prce and Josip Speranca.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, that is clear, and this document is already exhibited. We have seen it several times in the courtroom, and I think in the past weeks we have a report by Mr. Prce on his temporary work in the Main Staff and with respect to the establishment of the Home Guard. So that is not being challenged.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Anyway, Mr. Pinjuh, on this second page, number 26, we have Zvonko Susec again, and it says assistant to chief for establishment and staffing; and then 27, Tomislav Naletilic, chief for establishment; and then 37, Zeljko Akrap, assistant for education and training; and there's nobody else there dealing with any of these two major groups, establishment and education and training in the Main Staff. Is that what one can conclude on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if you recall the establishment of the Main Staff dated September 1992, and you were presented that document during the examination-in-chief, the establishment of the Main Staff and under number 44, 46, 47, 48, you spoke about the existence of department -- the department for manpower level replenishment. And we have 75 functions in that document, and if you add up all the people working there and occupying one post, it would follow that the Main Staff establishment-wise ought to number about 100 persons. Did you analyse the document in that way?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No. But the Main Staff below it has the operative zones, and they have these same people or, rather, similar people engaged in similar work, and they have war brigades who have people working in these areas, an assessment of the plan, a proposal for a plan, and then the plan goes to the administration for mobilisation and defence, which draws up a plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, I don't wish to deal with that. I'm not challenging that at all. All I want us to do is to clarify certain matters because from your answers about the existence of a department within the Main Staff dealing with these matters, the Judges could draw the conclusion that the Main Staff had about 100 persons organised in different departments and that this functioned in a somewhat different way from what these documents show. So that's why I'm asking you, if you compare these documents now, the ones I'm showing you now with the establishment of the Main Staff itself, what would you have to say? Was the Main Staff -- were the manpower levels in the Main Staff replenished 100 percent?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I can't say on the basis of a telephone directory and this document here, which is, in my opinion, far more relevant than the telephone directory because we are dealing with a list of persons who have regulated status in the Main Staff and persons who do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Pinjuh, that's why I didn't show you the telephone directory alone. I showed you three documents, so if you look at all three of them together, and you can see that in November 1992 there were 20 people in the Main Staff including all the auxiliary staff, and that in March 1993 there were 32 employees employed full-time, including all the auxiliary staff. What would you as a person dealing with a maintenance of manpower levels in certain units have to say about the manpower levels in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, it may have been approximately the same as the manpower levels of the wartime units or even less.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Pinjuh. Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question, but I don't know if you are able to answer or not and since it was the Alaburic Defence that presented this document. We are talking about the telephone directory. It is P 1572. In the telephone directory, you are listed under page 4. You are in there. It's the Department of the Defence here. I see the head Bruno Stojic, deputy Slobodan Busic, and then I see Mladen Naletilic and then Veso Vegar. To your knowledge, what was Naletilic doing in the department of the defence, if you know? If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I regret that I don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Well -- for D5. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAHOTA
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I call on the Prosecutor, I believe the Registrar has an IC number to give.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution has finally submitted its list of documents to be tendered through witness Vegar Veso. This list shall be given Exhibit number IC 929. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, the Prosecution can begin its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honours. Good evening, counsel, everybody else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Pinjuh.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pinjuh, just to start off, I'd like to just quickly revisit one or two of the things that you've testified about so far. Now, the first thing, you responded to a question by General Praljak that with regard to conscripts who did not heed call-up papers or call-up orders, there was actually very little that could be done with regard to them. You recall that answer of yours or that topic?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it correct that the decree on the armed forces and then the other decrees pertaining to -- sorry, if I may interrupt myself. If I could just ask the usher if we could retain the documents of those binders. Thank you. My apologies, sir. If we can return to the question. Is it correct or do you know that the decree on the armed forces and then various other decrees pertaining to the HVO military affairs provided that not reporting or not heeding call-up orders constituted an offence; it was a crime?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And punishment was also prescribed for that offence; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I assume it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, isn't it also correct that the big problem with draft dodgers is that they go abroad, they run away, they hide, and that's why it's very hard to catch them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So actually, if you say there was very little that you could do, that doesn't mean that you wouldn't do anything if you could trace these people. It was simply a matter of you had to find them first; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: We couldn't trace them. We couldn't get at them, neither we nor the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, the next thing that I would just quickly and briefly touch upon, and for this if we could quickly go back to the documents in the binder provided to you by the Defence of Mr. Petkovic, and that's the binder that you were looking at previously. I'd like to refer you to the last document in that binder, and that is 2D 01352, the very last document in that binder. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: 01352, yes, that's correct. And, sir, that is the list of payment for the Defence Department and the Main Staff signed by Bruno Stojic, but we were looking at the very last document earlier, which pertains to the payment of the Main Staff or the payroll of the Main Staff. If you could just return or turn to that document, the very last one in that collection. Do you have it? And it starts off with Adem Zulovic. You see that as number 1, and then it goes to number 20. Now, sir, my question on this is, if you look through those 20 names, you will notice that the name of General Petkovic doesn't appear there or, for instance, the name of Miro Andric, who appears on later lists. My question to you is: Do you know who was paying for their salaries at this time?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I really can't answer this question because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, before stepping off that, do you know Mr. Miro Andric and General Petkovic, and then Miro Andric's brother Baz [phoen] Andric who will appear on the later lists, were they members of the HVO or were they members of the HV?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to interfere, and I do apologise to my learned friend, but could the foundation be laid for Mr. Miro Andric for the period in 1992 because he appears in the lists for 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't belabour this point. There are documents in evidence. I didn't trace them. I can trace them by tomorrow, which refers to him as being also on the Main Staff in 1992. But I won't be labour that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's step off that and --

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: To your question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, did you want to respond to that question, sir?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I met Mr. Petkovic, but I didn't know the other gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn for a moment to the Home Guards, and for this I'd like you to turn to document P 01746 in the Prosecution binder. Sir, before -- do you have the document in front of you? P 01746. I think it should have a little yellow tab. Now, before we look at that document, you recall that we've already looked twice at a previous document which was an order issued by Bruno Stojic on the 5th of February, 1993, on the formation of Home Guards units based on the decision and organisation of Home Guards. Do you recall that document that we looked at, the February order, 5 February order by Bruno Stojic to establish Home Guards units? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: For the record, that was document P 01424. Now, sir, if we can look at this document, P 1746. This is an order by Milivoj Petkovic dated 28 March, 1993, and if we read at the top: "Given that in most cases order number 01-254/93 of 8 February, 1993, which concerns the organisation of the Home Guard, has not fully implemented, and in order to ensure that it is organised as quickly and as well as possible, I hereby order, in collaboration with defence administrations, immediately set about implementing all tasks in the said order ..." Sir, my question to you is: This is General Petkovic issuing an order to all operational zones of the HVO -- or within the HZ-HB, and this pertains to the establishment of Home Guards units. Do you agree this is an order for the implementation of the original order by Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, on the establishment of temporary commands, if that's the order you are referring to, two officers, one non-commissioned officer to receive Home Guards, if they are put at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, in other words, this order demonstrates that an order by Bruno Stojic on the 2nd of February is translated into action within all the operational zones of the HZ-HB; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, when replying to this, I said that the head sent the order down his line and the chief of the Main Staff also sent almost the same order down his line, and the order states who had to do what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just -- we may get back to this in another context, but Milivoj Petkovic's order, wasn't that only made possible because there was an earlier order by Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No. One does not exclude the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to something totally different now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you the very first document in the Prosecution binder. That is document P 00020. P 0020. It's the very first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document is the 1991 survey of the population or the "national composition of the population, 1991 results for the republic by municipalities and populated areas." And I've only included an extract with regard to Citluk municipality, and if you go to the very last page of your document, and this page has not been translated into English because it isn't necessary, so in the B/C/S version, for the English speakers, it's also the last page of the B/C/S version. And sir, there we see Citluk. The total population for Citluk is shown in 1991 as 15.063 people, and of that amount - and if we just move two columns or three columns across - the total number of Croats is 14.623. Are those figures basically correct to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: They could be. I believe this comes from the statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, if we look in Citluk municipality in 1991, in the second column it says there were only 111 Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: It could be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And then only 19 Serbs and 17 Yugoslavs, also basically correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And 113 declared themselves as others. Now, sir, stating the obvious, and I think you've also said this, but Citluk municipality was essentially inhabited exclusively by people of Croat ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you this data presented in a different format, and this is in the second-last document in your binder. It's P 10851. P 10851. And this is a map that was prepared after the 1991 census, and there was such a map basically for each municipality. Now, first of all, if we look at the top above the map, we'll see the figures, once again, Croats, 14.823; Serbs, 19; Muslims, 111; Yugoslavs, 17; and others, 113. So that corresponds with the previous document that you saw. That's correct; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the map itself, is that basically a map of Citluk in the middle?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the map is full of red circles, and if we look at the legend above, which says Croats, 14.823, it shows that Croats are indicated by red circles. So this, once again, shows that Citluk is basically inhabited by Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we look at the municipality to the south of Citluk. That's Capljina municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And we see that in Capljina municipality, to the eastern side of Capljina municipality there are a number of green dots. Is it correct that that basically corresponds to the area where the Dubravad [phoen] plateau lies? Is that basically where the Dubravad plateau lies, sir? I see you're shaking --

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes. Well, more or less, yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the green dots, if we look at the legend, they represent people of Muslim ethnicity showing that on the Dubravad plateau, Muslims stayed and lived; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those Muslims during the course of 1993 who stayed on the Dubravad plateau?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: To the west of Citluk, is that municipality basically Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And we see there's a small concentration of Muslims, and if we look very carefully, we'll see that that town where that dot is is Gradska. Do you know what happened to the Muslims in Gradska during 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: No, I really can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if you don't know what happened to these Muslims in the municipalities adjoining Citluk, why is that? Were you only focused on the events in Citluk or -- where you had functions to perform?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, we had so much work to do, you can see from these reports that we didn't -- well, that we barely had time to do them properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What happened to the 111 Muslims who resided in Citluk during 1993? Were they still there by the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I think most of them were, and I think they are still there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you receive any order to arrest any military-aged Muslim males during Citluk in 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I never received such an order, of course, because in 1991 we had units established which included Muslims, and in 1992 we knew that the army of BH was being established, and the Muslims went over to those units, and we did not make a fuss about that, nor did they make a fuss if someone moved from the BH Army into the HVO. So to the best of our knowledge, their conscripts are either in the BH Army or in third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying my best to abide by the rules. I did not intervene before the witness answered, but we should really have some grounds for this question. The witness testified about what he was doing, so was he someone who could issue orders of the kind my learned friend is asking about, and could he know based on his work in the office for defence about all these events?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just briefly respond. The witness being involved in defence matters should know about these matters or at least have an idea if such orders were being received or executed in the municipality where he worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you did not arrest any -- or do you know of any Muslim males who were arrested within Citluk municipality during or from the 30th of June, 1993, onwards?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, not then or later either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any Muslim women, children, or elderly who were expelled from Citluk municipality from July 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: I don't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So certainly you must have heard that Muslim males were arrested, military-aged men were detained from the 30th of June onwards by the HVO in places such as Gretelj [phoen] and Gabela? Sorry, is there a problem with the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems there's problem with the translation. Isn't it coming through? It's taking time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, informally I heard that there were some military prisons, but where they were, I didn't know, nor was it my job to know and what sort of prisons they were, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. What about the expulsion of women and children and elderly -- Muslim women, children, and elderly persons from municipalities such as Capljina and Stolac? Didn't you hear about that, or didn't you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know anything officially, but there were rumours going around, so it's very hard for me to comment on this really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just before stepping off of this map, if we look at the very centre of this map we see a dot, a big dot saying Citluk, and that's the town of Citluk. Was that where you were based?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes. The Citluk defence office was in the town of Citluk itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if we go north-east from there to Mostar, it appears that that is totally Croat-controlled territory; is that correct? If we look at the red dots, judging by them.

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, does that -- can we deduce from that that there were basically also good communications from Mostar to Citluk?

utterances.speaker: BRUNO PINJUH
